subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF AND INCREASE IN GUARANTEED LOANS
speechtext:
!
appreciate this opportunity to speak on Bill C-28, to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. As I look at this bill I have certain concerns. Fisheries plays a very important role in the economy of my riding, Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands. I do not wish to cover the waterfront in my talk; however, I do want to concentrate on one or two features.
First of all, I want to endorse the remarks of my colleague, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller), when he spoke about undisciplined overcapitalization. The cliche that we usually apply to this-and like all cliches, it has a degree of truth in it-is: Too much gear chasing too few fish. The fact that there is too much gear chasing too few fish is hurting fishermen.
Different answers are proposed to this dilemma, and one of them is the salmonid enhancement program, a program which we endorse. While we endorse the idea of the salmonid enhancement program as providing the possibility of more fish, we do not understand how the government can be proposing that program and at the same time failing to protect adequately fish habitat where these same salmon will be growing.
The hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) referred to the need for a more adequate program to protect
our estuaries. I am very concerned about the Cowichan estuary in my riding. It was two years ago that a task force was appointed by the provincial government on which the federal department of fisheries had representation. That task force heard numerous submissions for the citizens of the Cowichan area and from environmental groups desiring to protect that estuary from increased industrialization. Estuaries are easy places on which to expand industries, but we are only beginning to recognize the tremendous potential of estuaries for producing life and protein, and the place they occupy in the life cycle of many fish. Increased industrialization of the estuary involves land fill and dredging. This will be harmful to fish habitat.
While we have been waiting for two years for the report of the task force to be handed down, we have seen many small examples of this movement for increased industrialization going on apace. Log booms are more prevalent now than they were five years ago, and they are found outside their established leased areas. The destruction to estuaries because of log booms is becoming more and more known.
I should like to raise the following question with the hon. members and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc): What has the Department of Fisheries and Oceans been doing in order to protect this estuary? Where is the report of this task force? What has the department been doing to reassure the people who are fighting for the life of this estuary? When I meet with people who are involved in trying to save this estuary from industrialization, I realize that they are becoming discouraged; they are becoming disillusioned with coming before government with petitions and letters. They are beginning to wonder about the whole political process. In good faith two years ago, they put their submissions before the task force, yet the report has not been tabled. I should like the federal department to use some of its clout to get the provincial government to table that report. At the very least the department should move to reassure the people of the Cowichan Valley that there will be no further industrialization which in any way will adversely affect fish habitat.
We on the Pacific coast are very much concerned with the threat of increased tanker traffic. When tanker traffic is increased, not only is the danger of eco-disasters increased, but inevitably the day-by-day increment of seepage and small spills is increased, and this has a very detrimental effect upon our fisheries. Quite frankly, we are not happy with the very inadequate response so far from the government.
As we look at the salmonid enhancement program, we are happy that it exists, but we wonder what the point is of trying to provide this program. On the one hand, while on the other we do not preserve the existing fish habitat.
That brings me to the question of the bill before us which will provide more capital for more gear. What is the point of providing this capital unless we are willing to protect the existing fish habitat?
As I pointed out, the fact that we have too much gear chasing too few fish is hurting our fishermen. One group of fishermen that is being hurt the most is the Indian people.
June 5, 1980

They are being squeezed out of an industry in which they have always played a very key role. In fact, the entire culture and civilization of the native people along the Pacific coast has been dependent upon the resources of the sea. I am not only referring to the native people on the Pacific coast of British Columbia, but to those right from California north to Alaska. This is one of their aboriginal rights.
When the reserves were being set up for the people of British Columbia, instead of the larger reserves that are found in other parts of the country, the reserves for coastal Indians were very small. It was recognized that they faced out toward the sea and got their living from the sea, in large part, rather than from the land. In the early years of this century, a federal-provincial commission, the McKenna-McBride commission, recognized this fact and urged that certain plots of oceans and certain streams be put aside for the exclusive use of the native Indian people. This indicates the historic relationship between the Indian people and the fishery of our coast.
When the commercial fishing industry was first established in British Columbia, it depended very heavily upon native Indian people for labour. As those people began to relate to the impinging white culture, they came to depend very heavily upon commercial fishing as their means of livelihood. Now they are being squeezed out of this industry; they are being left behind. One trend that is taking place now-and it has taken place over a number of years-is that many of the small canneries on river inlets were shut down. They were moved to central places like Namu and Prince Rupert. Now the cannery at Namu has been closed and Prince Rupert has less of an industry than before. More and more of the fishing industry is being concentrated in the lower mainland of British Columbia. Not only is this leaving the native people behind and leaving no economic base for their communities, but it is a tremendous waste of our human resource. Also it is a very energy-intensive kind of centralization. At a time when we in Canada are facing an energy crisis, perhaps we should be asking questions as to whether this is the route we should be going. It is a waste of human resources and a waste of our energy resources.
The native people of British Columbia have a growing population, a young population. Increasingly these young people find that there is no place for them in the fishing industry. An industry which provided work for their parents and their grandparents has no place for them. Also we can look at the rising suicide rate, the rising crime rate and the rising rate of illness, and we do not need to ask too many questions about some of the reasons for this. The unemployment rate among young native people on the Pacific coast is directly related to their lack of opportunity in the fishing industry.
There are several reasons why they are being squeezed out. First of all, we can point to the failure of our educational programs and the failure to help these young people cope with new developments in technology and in managerial skills.
Second, we can point to the licensing program which was introduced by a Liberal government some ten years ago. At that time the minister of fisheries talked about getting rid of
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
some of the marginal people in the fishing industry. Perhaps these people were marginal from the point of view of the western empire, and perhaps they were marginal from the point of view of the Canadian fishing company before it became marginal itself; but I want to assure the House that these fishermen were not marginal from the point of view of their communities and they were not marginal from the point of view of their own families. They were the mainstay of these communities and the mainstay of their own families. What we have done with our licensing program is crowded them, not only out of their margins, but pushed them right off the edge. This licensing program has not accomplished its own stated objectives, but it has very effectively helped to squeeze the native people out of the fishing industry in British Columbia. Again there is a problem resulting from the lack of capital. Does this act help native Indian people in its terms? I suggest it does not.
Along with native groups I am glad the minister has indicated he intends to restore funds for the native fisheries assistance plan. 1 think that is good, but we need to realize this is a very small group of fishermen who will be helped in this way. In this connection, I would like to read a letter 1 received from a young Indian woman. It states in part:
We are a young couple trying to stand on our feet, but with a lot of hindrance from the fisheries and the licence system we are now without a licence for our trolier, we have no way to make a living. We have wrote letters to Sol Sinclair, who was supposed to have worked on the "B" licences. So far he has gotten nowhere. We weren't able to save enough money to purchase an "A" licence because of the income tax we have to pay.
She continues:
My words may not be strong enough to affect or get heard by anyone. But at least I am trying. I would like your opinion on what I am saying. Also who can help us. My husband and I have a lot of pride, we don't want to resort to welfare cheques.
This very moving letter I think speaks for a lot of young Indian people who would like to be able to have a stake in the fishing industry in British Columbia, who would like to be able to build and plan their lives with some pride and dignity. This legislation does nothing to help them and, indeed, there is no legislation or program I have seen which will help them.
The Native Brotherhood in British Columbia has submitted a brief to the minister outlining some of their concerns in this area. In this regard they say:
In the case of coastal Indians historically and presently dependent upon the fisheries resources of British Columbia, there is an obvious requirement to guarantee continued and increased opportunities in all aspects of the fishing industry.
This is a prerequisite for meaningful participation in the economic activities of the areas in which Indians live and for achieving a measure of control over their own social, cultural and economic destiny.
The brief goes on to state:
The response of both the Ministry of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Indian Affairs-both key departments in so far as Indians in British Columbia are concerned-to the above priorities, related programs and funding, is one of nominal support for the self-development concept. However, in practice, the efforts of departmental personnel and the programs initiatied are severely restricted in their scope and potential for achieving true self-development.

June 5, 1980
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act
There is nominal support but there is little real help, f would ask this government, through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and in conjunction with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to bring into this House a comprehensive program to ensure the place of the Indian fisherman in British Columbia.

subsubtopic: EXTENSION OF AND INCREASE IN GUARANTEED LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to cause any nervous spasms over on the other side, and I do promise after I have made a comment or two to make certain that this bill is allowed to go through before five o'clock. However, I think this is an opportunity for me to deal with a matter of pretty grave importance to a lot of the people I represent along the Fraser River system in British Columbia, and I want to say one or two words about their present concerns while the parliamentary secretary to the minister is in the House. I do not suggest I am going to come up with any great profundities related to solutions to the problems of concentration of ownership, habitat destruction, or the loss of wetlands for spawning grounds which is occurring all over the country, especially on the west coast as it applies particularly to the salmon fishery.
1 will say, however, that there seem to be signs that the salmon fishery in British Columbia is on the decline because of the concentration of very advanced and highly capitalized fishing and hunting equipment. The people 1 represent, or some of them, especially those who are engaged in a special kind of river fishery, are in fact the last in line when it comes to the distribution of the catch. Consequently, in addition to the suspicions that abound when people's livelihoods are at stake, through the natural competition within the industry, and from foreign sources, again with highly efficient and efficacious gear, there is within the fishery a natural suspicion that I think needs to be explored and perhaps laid to rest because it is based on facts and on rumours. I do not think we can ignore the fact that it exists whether factually based or not.
We have had in the Fraser River fishery this year only six openings for spring salmon, and these openings have occurred approximately once a week. To date there have been six, and last year by this time there were 17. To date we have caught 2,600 fish. That is the total catch for Fraser River gill netters.
Because the gill netter is the last in line, if there is overfishing by foreign fleets or by our own domestic fleets with other kinds of methods, set up in different ways, such as the trailers and seiners, the catch of these fishermen is much reduced.
This situation was described, I thought very eloquently, by my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly). He described these radio-controlled, fast, efficient fishing machines which, once an opening was called, raced from one point to another in a moment, practically, in terms of the season, rapidly depleting that particular area as it is declared open. This has led to overcapitalization with larger and larger vessels costing more and more money, employing fewer and fewer people. That seems to be the story of our life.
1 would not want to occur in British Columbia the kind of demand that occurred in Newfoundland where the inshore fisheries were declared at one point to be redundant, and the only salvation for the Newfoundlander was to move him into large communities, destroying his particular culture and way of life, taking what was once an independent, self-reliant family living in a small village, to which he could relate, and making another welfare case in a larger vicinity.
It is very important, I think, in our headlong rush to greater and greater efficiency that we also keep in mind that there is a human factor, and that the large, advanced fishing machines do not pay for very much at the local store. We must remember that the destruction of many small, independent communities is the result of what we call our headlong rush to modernization. 1 think the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) would agree that the same thing has happened to some extent, perhaps to a large extent, in prairie areas which he represents.
Many, many monuments to the initiative and self-reliance of individuals have been destroyed as the smaller towns disappear because of larger farms. That seems to have been the trend in the last quarter of the twentieth century. We must make certain that there is a place for people and that that place will provide self-fulfilling and useful occupations. We must make certain that we do not allow ourselves, through various kinds of government initiatives, such as the bill we were discussing now, to allow people to be displaced and misplaced.
What is happening as a result of the intense competition within the groups of seiners, trawlers and gill netters and the foreign competition which has already been alluded to in this debate is that the industry is experiencing practically a fish war on both coasts. There have been instances in Alaska where declarations of open fishing in certain parts of shared waters have been such that the fisheries department has-and I hope that this is not too strong a word-unleased Canadian fishermen. In other words, it has removed the discipline of our conservation measures to the point where Canadian fishermen are competing wholesale with American fishermen and intercepting fish bound for American rivers.
The Americans may retaliate if this kind of thing is allowed to proceed and if we are unable to reach an agreement on both coasts with regard to this commonly shared, natural, renewable resource. This bill is not a matter of small consequence. Unless we can get ratification through the U.S. Senate in a relatively short period of time, we will be back at square one. In the meantime, we may have lost a resource or so seriously damaged it that it will take years to recover it, at a time when the demand for protein is increasing as populations grow. 1 do not think that we can afford that kind of frivolous, unco-operative management of a resource which is so valuable not only to Canada and the U.S. but to the world.
When these closures, such as the one which I described as the beginning of my remarks, result, fishermen on the Fraser River who have a large investment in gear, who must meet these investments and who are denied an opportunity to recoup
June 5, 1980

this investment-in other words, to pursue their livelihood- are the ones who lose. We must realize, though, that there must be a certain amount of escapement or there will be no tomorrow for the fishing industry.
There are at least three advisory committees to the ministry of fisheries on the Pacific coast. There is an advisory committee in the north, an advisory committee to the sockeye commission, which is an international commission, and an advisory committee for the Frasher fisheries. At the moment these committees do not make reports publicly. Their recommendations to the ministry do not, in the normal course of events, see the light of day in the public press. The reports are not published and distributed to the fishermen, unless it is through the fishermen's union paper and, of course, all fishermen, particularly gill netters, do not necessarily belong to the fishermen's union.
I would like to pay tribute once again to the kinds of things that have been happening in the enhancement program. However, besides underlining the gravity of the problems in the British Columbia salmon fishery at the moment, I suggest that we try to obtain the co-operation of the groups involved and make certain that the knowledge of the amount of catch, escapement, and the amount taken by native fishermen- which is their right-is made available on a regular basis and on a highly public basis within the industry, so that there can be a fair and equitable distribution among the people who are dependent upon this resource for their livelihood.
At the moment it is felt among the gill netters, the people I largely represent within the industry, that since they are the last in line and since they may possibly be, because they operate in the river, not as highly mechanized as other groups, that they are always asked to pay the price through early closures resulting from the excesses of others. They also feel there are not enough fisheries inspection officers or habitat control officers to make certain that their rights are protected, that the fish which they lose through escapement to the spawning grounds are, indeed, used efficiently once they get to the spawning grounds. This is because there is a lack of investment in proper spawning ground management and control.
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to say these few words on this subject. As far as my party is concerned, we are prepared to let the bill go through this stage.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak on this bill, but I do want to make one short point. I will be brief so that we can pass this bill before five o'clock. I want to highlight what is happening on the west coast in the fishing industry. As the hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) has indicated, some of the regulatory habits of the department of fisheries are frustrating the fishermen.
However, there is another aspect which I think should be brought to the attention of this House, and that is the pyramiding of corporate power, which is frustrating the independence of the fishermen. Fishermen by nature are independent
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act businessmen. When B.C. Packers bought out the Canadian Fish Company, it effectively left British Columbia with only one corporation with which the fishermen could deal. That means that the fishermen will be forever indentured to that one corporation. Such a move is very destructive of the fishing industry of that province.
Secondly, there used to be fishermen who were unhappy with B.C. Packers and moved over to Canadian Fish Company. Now that the Canadian Fish Company has been bought by B.C. Packers, these fishermen are, really, people without a country because there is nowhere for them to go. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and his parliamentary secretary must look at this situation because it is no good to pass a bill such as the one before us which extends the borrowing power and refinancing possibilities of fishermen if they have nowhere to go once they have refinanced their vessels.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to have this opportunity to speak, very briefly of course, in support of Bill C-28. The debate has been very interesting. I have listened with great interest, both today and yesterday, to all hon. members who spoke, and many good points were raised. However, many of the points were very global in nature and were not apropos the bill itself.
The bill increases the borrowing power from $75,000 to $150,000 for vessel construction or improvement. Certainly members who took part in the debate had very different views on what the bill would do and would not do for the fishery. There may have been some misunderstanding as to its purpose, but since the bill will go to committee, many of the questions will be answered at that time.
1 think one hon. member mentioned that the bill could influence and assist in corporate concentration of the fishery. Given the amount of money involved in this bill, it would probably work directly opposite to that suggestion simply because the purpose of the bill is to help the small independent fisherman. I do not have much more to say on the bill, with the exception that we will move it to committee.

I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and if 1 may be permitted I will continue the debate begun a few days ago on the motion introduced by my colleague the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). We were then talking about the classification of government employees and in that respect, 1 personally talked about what is called the red circling of employees. I explained the procedure we used so people would not be penalized as a result of the reclassification of their positions. With your permission, I will continue today to discuss that point and a few other matters.

Madam Speaker, in the earlier part of the motion the hon. member for Vaudreuil stated that the objective of the motion is to try to obtain more information on what is happening in the public service in the area of classification. It is to that point that I am going to address my remarks. I will attempt to respond to this request by outlining some of the more important changes Treasury Board has made to the policies and procedures governing classification in the public service.
As you may recall, Madam Speaker, the classification of 4,000 positions throughout the public service was conducted in two distinct phases. After the initial findings of the audit of the national capital area were communicated to the departments, Treasury Board continued with the audit outside the national capital area. In addition, Treasury Board undertook a pilot study of the classification system in the personnel policy branch of Treasury Board and in one operating department, as well as a detailed review of all policies and procedures related to classification in the public service.
These reviews indicated that there were significant problems in the conduct and management of, and results being realized from, the classification system as it stood. In terms of the quality of classification decisions, they indicated an unacceptable degree of overclassification; that is, putting people in a higher category than they should have been. As well, there was some underclassification and some allocation to the wrong occupational category or group. These were few and did not account for the high misclassification rate.
It was concluded that some of these problems were caused by attempts to use the classification system to solve problems in other personnel areas, such as recruitment and retention of personnel. Other problems were caused by the policies and procedures themselves.
Specifically, the classification was not-I repeat, not- designed to allow the classification of individual positions to, first of all, attract, reward, retain, sanction or remove employees. It was not designed to circumvent the intent of wage controls or bargained pay rates by reclassifying positions and individuals upwards. It was not designed to reflect perceived intergroup pay relativities. The common perception is that the pay relationships do exist between groups as well as incomes.

I was saying what the classification system was not designed to do and I had mentioned three things. Fourth, it was not designed to provide protection from the impact of reorganizations which result in a reduction in number of positions or responsibilities.
On December 18, 1978, the document entitled "Report on the Classification Audit in the National Capital Area and the Non-National Capital Area" was tabled in the House. As a result of this report and the review of all existing classification policies and procedures, Treasury Board moved systematically to revise its policies and procedures to overcome the problems and difficulties identified with classification in the public service. These changes to the policies and procedures are designed to improve the classification system and correct the misclassification of positions.
In summary, the various changes and actions undertaken by the Treasury Board are as follows. The Treasury Board advised all departments and agencies of the results of the special audit and instructed those with positions identified as misclassified to undertake corrective action. Wherever appropriate, the follow-up action was initiated by the Treasury Board and the process of correcting the misclassified positions has now been completed. In terms of information, this should be pleasing to the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert).
The Treasury Board secretariat began a review of the classifications systems and procedures in all departments and agencies and in 1979-80 completed the review in 10 departments. Each department is required to prepare an action plan in response to the recommendations made and the secretariat monitors these plans to ensure that corrective action is taken.
The Treasury Board secretariat reviewed all occupational
groups identified in the audit report as having special problems
Classification Audit
and has initiated corrective action. The board withdrew from all departments and agencies the authority to classify positions in the higher levels of the personnel administration, financial administration, economics, sociology and statistics groups. These proposed new positions or classification level changes in these cases are submitted for final decision to Treasury Board. Treasury Board has established specific procedures and time frames for correcting any misclassification. Here it must be understood that great strides have been taken to correct any misclassification areas which were built into the system. I am proud of the progress that has been made over the last short period of time.
In conclusion, over the past few years the administration and the policies and procedures of the classification system of the public service have been subjected to a comprehensive and detailed review-the first such detailed review since the current system was put in place-which has brought about an improvement and strengthening of the administration of the classification system of the public service of Canada.

I had some discussion in the last week or two with various individuals concerning the difference between the position of a member of Parliament and the position of a senator. When a report is tabled in this House, that is effectively the end of the discussion. There is no means by which the member of Parliament can continue the debate, in committee or in the House, or to pressure the government to report on progress, whereas in the Senate they have their own means to continue the debate on the subject as they desire.
In the future when we change the system in this House, we must find some means by which we have continuing discussion on the various reports that are tabled.
1 would like to list three reports to which I referred earlier to indicate why it is so necessary that we have something from the government on the progress they made either in implementing recommendations or in deciding not to take action, and if they decide not to take action, we should know that.
The first report to which I referred was tabled in this House on Thursday, February 26, 1976, by myself as co-chairman of the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations

Mr. Chairman, I certainly do not agree with the Cassandra-like prophecies of the hon. member. I am a little surprised that he wants to dwell so distinctly, in the depth of gloom and doom that he seems to be prescribing. As someone who has some acquaintanceship with the technicalities of projection and economic forescasting, he would know that the kind of precision for which he is asking is not possible, it is absolutely impossible to predict, to the exact month, what the unemployment rates will be. There are far too many factors and variables to take into account. He mentioned some of them himself.
We are certainly subject to variations, whether it is on exchange rates, interest rates, downturns in the international economy, varying degrees of supply and demand rates, programs of intervention that may take place, investment procedures, and while those things can be built into certain kinds of computations on an aggregate scale, I do not think anyone has a scale to pinpoint absolutely that, let us say, on January 15 there will be 973,000 unemployed, and that is why we tend to use percentages, because it is a better indicator of the kind of general patterns that we have to face in the economic forecast. Those patterns and indications were provided for in the statement of the Minister of Finance. I should point out, just to make sure that the record is perfectly clear, that those projections that the present Minister of Finance was making were not quite as severe as those that were predicted by the minister of finance under the previous administration, who was predicting, at that point in time, excess unemployment of 200,000 people, beginning in 1981-82.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad the hon. member asked that question, because I think it does pertain to the kind of planning that we are doing. As I stated in the House earlier, one of the serious difficulties we faced when we resumed government was the fact that the previous administration had basically wiped out many of the direct job-creation programs. So there was nothing in preparation, nothing available for us to bring to bear on the cycle of unemployment which we face in this country. Certainly, in the historical sense, we know that unemployment peaks, in this country, during the winter months. That is why we had to introduce a program of which the hon. member was, unfortunately, critical. We had to introduce a program in an interim way that could be announced in June, so that it could start in operation in the fall so that it would be fully operative through the months of December, January and February, when seasonal unemployment is at its highest.
As I admitted in the House, we had to put together a program that did not give us the kind of time that we would have liked, simply because the cupboard was bare, there was nothing to bring forward. As a consequence, the programs and the budget and the estimates for that program had some limitations to them.
But to answer that question, that is why we have designed a program, as we have, to begin operation in September of this coming year, to reach its peak in providing specific targets into high unemployment areas beginning throughout the winter months, when unemployment tends to be at its highest.
But I should also like to point out to the hon. member that, in a way, we should not get ourselves lulled into believing that we can simply respond to seasonal variations, because one of the underlying philosophies of our own direct job-creation program is to tackle the hard core unemployment, whether it is in the youth sector or in the sector of people who have a minority status in this country. If you look at the figures, the way the labour market turns around in this country, there is a fair degree of fluctuation and mobility within that market.
The most severe difficulties are faced by those who are, in a sense, permanently unemployed, because they cannot get the first entry into the job market. That is why we are increasingly orienting our own investments and our own practices towards tackling that hard-core problem. It may be only 10 per cent of the young people who are the hard-core unemployed. The rest, eventually, over a period of time, find jobs. That is why we have to target, particularly on training programs, target in particularly on those who need first entry experience.

Mr. Chairman, I would say it is some of both. As a trained sociologist, which I believe he is, he would
certainly be aware of the kind of studies and analyses that have been produced in the last several years. Perhaps the most pronounced and comprehensive study was the OECD study, about two years ago, which indicated that the problem of youth unemployment is not just a Canadian problem. It is a problem shared by every country in the industrial world. We are, frankly, facing a product of a population boom which took place, for example, after the Second World War. In fact, in Canada, we have had, unquestionably, the largest growth in the number of young people in the job market, over the last seven or eight years, of any country in the industralized world. It is a problem we share.
As well, as a sociologist, the hon. member would know that the handicaps people face in the job market are partly a product of their own environment. Lack of education is an obvious difficulty for those who grow up in a region where they do not acquire skills or educational capacities, for whatever reason. Sometimes it is a product of geography. Unfortunately and tragically there are regions of our country where there is not much of an economic base upon which to build jobs.
Some of my colleagues in this caucus have brought their constituents to see me. For example, the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria brought a group of people to see me who were honest, hard-working, dedicated people. They wanted to work in his region of the country and there was just not the economic base there to provide employment. They spend most of their summers travelling to do agricultural work in Ontario, but when they return to their home areas in New Brunswick, simply there is no work for them. That is one of the reasons why we went into direct job creation, to ensure that they would have opportunities to work if they wanted to do so. The hard core areas of unemployment are products of population problems which are shared industrially throughout the entire world. Partly they are a product of geography and individual deficiencies, sometimes not of a person's own making, such as family characteristics or whatever. In this situation we see substantial changes taking place. That is why we have entered into a very major review of the employment issues of the 1980s.
We have asked for a parliamentary committee to be formed under the chairmanship of the Honourable Warren Allmand. I believe the hon. member will be a member of that committee. It will be an opportunity for parliamentarians to cross this country in order to look at and assess the problems of shortages, and unemployment issues across Canada, in a public manner. We have put together a major task force of my own commission on employment and immigration. We are pulling together people from different departments in the government to begin to understand what changes are taking place in our economic structure, so that we can put together a proper design which will enable the government, provincial government and the private sector to begin to combine their efforts more effectively to meet the new employment demands and requirements of the next decade. In the meantime we have this

interim program to make sure we can handle the short-term problems.
That is one of the things 1 felt very strongly about when 1 took over this portfolio. I realized that we had to do a very careful review and analysis of the kinds of things we had to look forward to, so that we could change the programs which required change and put together a package of employment initiatives and partnership within the public and private sectors.

If the hon. member feels insecure, disturbed, and overwrought by the lack of the presence of some public servants on the floor of the House, then 1 would be very glad to provide them. 1 would not want to be the cause of a nervous breakdown of the hon. member for Calgary West, but I would suggest that he is receiving exactly the answers deserving of the kinds of questions he is asking.

Mr. Chairman, there are a number of things on which I would like to seek a response from the minister this evening regarding problems of unemployment for which the employment tax credit bill ostensibly proposes to provide a solution, at least partly.
In my riding of Winnipeg-Birds Hill just last week there were a number of employees of the Canadian National Railway, some 49 at Transcona shops and another five at the Symmington yard, who were laid off their jobs, and there is a similar number scheduled to be laid off in the coming weeks. Indeed there are rumours of even more lay-offs.
1 should like to ask the minister, in view of his concern about unemployment, what the government, and what he in his capacity as minister of employment, are doing about this latest move of the Canadian National Railroad in abandoning its extensive hiring and expansionist intentions of only a few months ago and now proceeding to lay people off? I ask this particularly in view of Canada's high unemployment rate, certainly much higher than any of the statistics being tossed about tonight would indicate: Unemployment is higher than those statistics if we consider the hidden unemployment and the tremendous concentration of unemployment, not just in various regions but in various parts of our cities.
I should like to ask the minister what he thinks himself capable of doing in respect of this latest action of the CNR, taking into account particularly the unfairness of hiring people, creating expectations of permanent employment, only to lay those people off in a short time, facing them again with economic uncertainty. Will the minister undertake to speak with his colleagues, the Minister of Transport and the hon. gentleman in the other place, who may or may not be responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, to see whether the CNR could use this time to catch up on its repair work, repairing all the many grain cars and hopper cars that require repair, continuing the employment of people in this important enterprise, rather than contributing to the unemployment problem we have by allowing these layoffs?

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member's question is very important, but I am not sure I would judge it as relevant to this bill.
The issue of lay-offs in railway yards is one that would give those of us who live in the Winnipeg area some concern. 1 would ask the hon. member to treat it with some degree of perspective. As long as I have been living in Winnipeg the railways have been laying people off and hiring people. It is a
cyclical industry; it goes up and down according to the season. 1 have not read of massive lay-offs by the railways. If I remember the figures accurately, the railroads in Winnipeg have been very consistent employers with a reasonably stable work force.
If the hon. member is asking what measures I am taking, I would draw his attention to the initiative that we announced only last Friday. Through the co-operation of several of my colleagues we were able to put forward a major proposal for the city of Winnipeg to create substantial renovation and rejuvenation of the core area, including work in some of the railroad yards, both CN and CPR, if that is the choice of the city. This will create several thousand jobs in Winnipeg over the next five or six years. Already we have taken substantial action to provide a major stimulus to the employment situation in Winnipeg.
I would like to thank the hon. member and some of his colleagues in the NDP caucus for their support during the period when we were trying to get the kind of encouragement that was necessary to bring those measures about. This is one significant measure that will have a major and beneficial impact on the employment picture in Winnipeg.

Mr. Chairman, the minister knows just from listening to what I had to say that I was not trying to portray any sort of cataclysmic event happening at the CNR, but merely trying to draw his attention to a fact, a situation, in which I think management is making some errors of decision.
We have an opportunity to build up the grain car and hopper fleet of those railroads which are in the habit of saying they do not have the equipment to move the grain. The minute they experience a revenue drop they begin to cut back on their intentions to rebuild their fleets. I think this is something that would merit conversation with the president of the CNR, to discover why they are doing this, whether there might not be alternatives, and whether they might be able to put this time to better use.
My second concern, and it follows on something the minister said, has regard to what was announced last Friday in Winnipeg and, indeed, what was announced on Monday in regard to the employment strategy of the government.
The minister is overplaying the extent to which the announcement he had to make on Friday and, indeed, the announcement of Monday, are going to solve or even come close to solving the problems the city of Winnipeg is experiencing in many different respects. The program announced on Friday involves money, as I understand it, that is not going to come into play until 1981. There is going to be a study first, as if the core area of Winnipeg had not been studied enough, and as though we did not know what kinds of things need to be done there already. The minister in his former capacity presided over many studies, and I presume that if those studies had any quality we can go to them for recommendations on what should be done in the core area of Winnipeg. I think much is being made of little in the rhetoric we are hearing about what was announced on Friday. There has been no articulation of

how that money is going to be spent, what programs are to be in place, or any indication of just what form the spending of that money is to take. Until we hear that we cannot make a judgment as to whether, indeed, what was announced last Friday will address itself to the problems of Winnipeg.
Another aspect of the very same problem is related to unemployment in the inner city of Winnipeg. I read in the minister's speech of last Monday something about the Community Services Project, this new program which will do so many good things for the cities in which it is implemented. I suggest to the minister that this is very much a recycling of what existed before, the Canada Works plan. If it is intended to be an improvement of the Canada Works plan, 1 suggest it does not go anywhere near meeting the aspirations of those who have had experience with the Canada Works plan and know the inadequacies thereof.
There was a meeting in Winnipeg during the election. The hon. member for Provencher was there and perhaps he will recall it, at which a group presented recommendations for further employment programs in the inner city. One of the things they asked for was a three-year cycle in respect of any kind of program, whether it was to be called Canada Works or Community Services.
I notice that the three-year cycle of the Community Services Project is a diminishing three-year cycle. It is to be funded fully in the first year, and the percentage of funding is to diminish over the next two years. Certain conditions are attached to the programs to be funded in the first place and whether or not they are to be continued. An example of those conditions is whether they have any possibility of being sustained by user fees in the future, introducing the concept of user fees into social services. The minister should know from his experience in the city of Winnipeg that any program which is asked to be dependent on user fees in the inner city will not address the problems of that particular area. He should know that such a program will not address problems of unemployment.
' We have heard about rates of unemployment of 7 per cent, 8 per cent and 9 per cent. A study done by Winnipeg School Division No. 1 shows that among the adults around Dufferin school in the inner city of Winnipeg there is a 60 per cent unemployment rate. Also in the inner city around William Whyte school there is a 55 per cent unemployment rate, around David Livingston school a 45 per cent unemployment rate, around Norquay school in North Point Douglas there is a 44 per cent unemployment rate, and around Strathcona school across from where I used to work, Robertson House, there is a 39 per cent unemployment rate. There are 28 schools in whose areas there is a 13 per cent or greater rate of unemployment among the adults of the children who attend those schools.
Clearly the program which the minister announced on Monday will not address itself to these sorts of problems, and neither will the employment tax credit program. It is incumbent upon the minister not to mislead the public and say that

these programs will solve our problems, particularly when there is nothing within them which is geographically specific to address the particular problems of the inner city. For instance, the whole Community Services project is designed to continue the very problems which people for years have been asking be corrected in those kinds of employment programs.
What kind of problems should be corrected? We must get rid of certain problems and introduce programs so that there will be some security, so that people who embark upon jobs will know whether or not they will have that job next year at the same time, when the grant must be renewed. I notice that the community development aspect of the program is for a term of one year. This does nothing to eliminate the insecurity of working on these particular programs.
In the one program which is of a longer duration, three years, people will still have to look for other moneys every year because of the diminishing effect. The minister should know the problems which the community school's programs in the core area of Winnipeg had when it had to find money because the provincial government and the school board began to pull out. He should know the work that went into getting United Way funding for that particular program. This is exactly the kind of burden which the minister is laying on every project under the auspices of this Community Services project.
It is a grossly inadequate answer to the kinds of concerns which have been placed before the minister in his capacity as minister and in his capacity before he was elected, concerns of which the minister should be well aware. These are problems which have been apparent for years. I invite the minister's defence of these particular programs, and ask him not to indulge in the kind of hyperbole to which we have become accustomed in listening to him describe his initiatives. Would the minister tell us how these particular programs will solve the problems of the 60 per cent and 55 per cent of the people who are unemployed in some of the areas around the inner city schools?
I hope that the minister will not try to tell us about the great things which will happen because of the announcement that he made last Friday, because it is not clear, and it will not be clear for some time, whether that money will be used to redevelop the core area of Winnipeg for the benefit of the low income citizens of Winnipeg, the tenants and the people who inhabit that area, or whether it is to be channelled according to the dictates of the 1CEC on city council. The things which have just occurred to me that I would like to say about the ICEC, Mr. Chairman, would be unparliamentary, and 1 had to pause for a moment. It is not clear how this money will be spent and whether it will in any way be beneficial to the people who are unemployed to this great extent.

They were there and they had the opportunities, the commitments and the resources.
1 would also like to remind the hon. member that the initiative that we took on Friday was the first major social economic initiative in the inner city that has been taken by a major government, including the hon. member's provincial government which was NDP for eight years.
1 do not wish to debate the point, but I think that it is important that the hon. member understand and that we exchange thoughts in a reasonable way. The problems of hard core unemployment will not be solved overnight. I did not say that they would be in my statement in Winnipeg on Friday, nor in my statement in this House on Monday. 1 said that we must work at these problems with all the resources at our command, but I did not say that they would be solved right away. These problems have been with us far too long and in far too many ways.
Any government is restricted by the kinds of resources that it can bring to bear, because there are demands from across the country, not just from the inner city of Winnipeg, but from the northeast corner of New Brunswick, the Gaspe of Quebec, northern Ontario and Athabasca. There are unemployment problems of a hard core nature which have been around for years because of the very nature of the economy and the geography of our country. I can tell hon. members that I will work as hard as 1 can.

To answer the question, Mr. Chairman, 1 must say there is no geographic limitation at all. The bill applies right across Canada. The only requirement is that it must be an employer who makes the application. In the initial evaluation we found that about 60 per cent or 70 per cent of the applications are from employers with less than 20 employees, so it tends to be the smaller employers who use the program with the greatest frequency. This means that certain regions of the country use it less because they do not have the employment base, so that there is some regional variation. It is applicable across the country, however.

Mr. Chairman, many of the questions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North were presented earlier on in the discussions. I will briefly summarize the answers I made at that time. To begin with, as I said, we are presently engaged in a major review of the employment requirements in Canada in the next decade and how we can best answer them. We have established a parliamentary committee to look at that. It will be composed of members from all sides of the House. We have established a major task force in our department.
As I indicated in my statement, 1 hope to have a paper available which can be presented and tabled in Parliament by the end of this year, and then we could have a major discussion about the employment strategies which should be followed. Very many changes are taking place. In the last ten years we have been relying upon ideas about job creation at which I want to have a new look. I intend to have a new look at them. We will welcome the participation of the hon. member in that parliamentary committee, so that we can come to grips with many of the new changes which are taking place.
He mentioned the problem of industrial dislocation which is taking place in the automobile industry. I assure the hon. member that we are presently meeting with the UAW-and have over the past several weeks-to work out programs to develop income support and assistance. We have had very cordial relationships with UAW in working out those common problems. But this is a new problem which has never been experienced in the industrial heartland before. We are aware of it, and we want to provide a solution which has been worked out with the unions and employers involved. That is what we are engaging in right now.
I can assure the hon. member that we are looking at a new strategy. We will be consulting with a wide variety of organizations. If he is the member from his caucus who sits on this parliamentary committee, then he will have a full opportunity to travel across Canada and hear the briefs and representations from various organizations. He can apply his own wisdom and experience to the problem. This is something we intend to do. In the meantime, as I have said, we are faced with a very major problem of creating work in the short-term, so that we have something available for Canadians while this review is taking place. That is why we announced the programs on Monday.
They are not necessarily the total strategy, but they are indicators of the kind of direction in which we would like to go, the kind of incentives we are offering employers to provide
work for women in non-traditional work. There is increasing emphasis upon training programs, particularly the additional $10 million which is a 50 per cent increase in that program for native people to begin working on native projects. Those are the kinds of areas we want to go into.
We are establishing an experimental program of local economic development. It will have 15 to 18 to 20 pilot projects across Canada. They will provide long-term jobs and economic development across Canada. We could not get into a massive program of that kind until we saw how it actually worked. But we put enough money into our spending to provide a wide variety of long-term community economic development programs in communities across the country. As we evaluate them as part of our over-all review, and if they seem to have real promise, then we will incorporate them in a much larger way.
We are using our job-creation programs that we announced on Monday to provide us with an indicator of where we might go to deal with contemporary and future problems in the employment field. These are problems which developed not while the minister was in office but while his party and his colleagues were in office.
Let me list some of those problems very quickly. I know we will have lots of time to discuss them on other occasions. It is now obvious, as many people have been pointing out for years, that our whole industrial strategy, or lack of strategy, has meant that our major manufacturing organizations, which are Canadian subsidiaries of multinational corporations, have been geared not to be so efficient that they are able to compete for
June 5, 1980

their share of the market not just in Canada but on the international level. The result is that they are now being battered and destroyed, not only for international markets but right here in Canada. The Liberal government of the past has done nothing for that.

We are not even beginning to do the job. There is nowhere we can see that more vividly than in the minister's and my city of Winnipeg. It has been estimated by educators in Canada that three million people, speaking from memory, but 1 think, if anything, I am underestimating, in this country are functionally illiterate.
We have noted in the city of Winnipeg the movement of native people from their reserves to the city, as well as to the city of Regina and others. They feel they will be better living in the cities than on the reserves where they were born. ENERGY CONSERVATION-INQUIRY WHETHER LEGISLATIVE ACTION PROPOSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 26 and May 27 I asked some questions of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) regarding certain documents which I had in my possession, one a confidential document from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources policy and analysis sector, and the other a transcript of an interview with the assistant deputy minister of energy, Mr. Clark. These statements were of concern to me because of the obvious problems which were noted in those documents with regard to the department wanting to get the nation off oil and on to other non-renewable energy sources.
At the same time they were considering that policy they were saying that they could not have two policies, one dealing with getting the nation off oil and one dealing with conservation of energy. The minister said that he was not aware of those statements within his department, and that is why I wanted to carry this debate on more fully this evening. I want to quote some of the statements which were made within these documents. One is from a source within the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources which states that:
-policy rationale within EMR is getting narrower and narrower. The decisionmaking balance is off keel. Though conservation will still make advances, the heavy emphasis on off-oil has gone beyond what reasonable economic analysis would allow.
Mr. Clark, the assistant deputy minister, stated in response to that:
-you don't want to give the public too many confusing signals so you really have to decide whether you are telling them to get off oil or are you telling them to conserve energy.
That does not show much faith in the intelligence of the Canadian people. He goes on to say:
Since in the short run what we really want them to do is to get off oil, we ought to concentrate our communications efforts on getting them off oil rather than conserving energy.
This is of deep concern to me because there is such a quick and cheap supply of energy available to Canada through the conservation policy. When the assistant deputy minister makes statements like this, it makes me wonder about the policies of the department.
Mr. Clark goes on to say:
-it would be nice to conserve all sorts of energy but it does seem to me-at least my advertising people tell me-
Is the department now considering its policy through its advertising department? Mr. Clark goes on:
June 5, 1980

-that it is difficult if the public gets different messages. So our conservation campaign concentrates on saying let's conserve oil. First get off oil. Then start to conserve-
Those statements are astonishing. One of the bureaucrats in the department said in response:
The feds have very little money yet they are going to spend it on substituting to another non-renewable fuel.
This document states that the off-oil policy is to get people off oil and onto natural gas, which is fine if we are prepared for that kind of program. The bureaucrat went on to say:
This will not result in much public confidence. But Clark doesn't know how to grapple with substitution to conservation and renewables.
The minister must get a hold on his department. If these kinds of statements are coming from the assistant deputy minister and are being contradicted by other officials in other sectors of the department, then how will this minister receive the proper advice which he needs from his department from time to time? I think he must get control of that department and tell them, as he told me in this House, that his policy is contrary to that and that he is concerned about conservation.
This government does not have a very good record in that area, Mr. Speaker. The report of the International Energy Agency of 1976 concluded that Canada's conservation record, over all, was one of the worst in the world. Our consumption of oil and natural gas per capita is the highest in the world. This waste of energy is costing us billions of dollars per year. If we could just get ourselves into a conservation frame of mind we could save hundreds of thousands of barrels of oil per day.
The Conservative party policy was to reduce consumption of oil and gas, or energy generally, by a 2 per cent factor per year but it seems as if the factor for this government as expressed in their document "Energy Conservation in Canada" is a 3.5 per cent increase per year. Between 1975 and 1990 the difference between the 2 per cent and 3.5 per cent factors would be from 482,000 to 600,000 barrels of oil per day. We just cannot overlook that, Mr. Speaker, and we must get serious about our conservation policy.
Through CHIP and by insulating the 70 per cent to 90 per cent of homes that are insulatable, by 1990 we could save another 104,000 barrels per day. There are many other ways that we could save on the energy that is necessary to meet our demands, through conservation programs in the coming years. 1 think the minister should answer my questions and tell us how serious he is about conservation.
Mir. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources): Mr. Speaker, I welcome the hon. member's support for the conservation efforts being made or planned by Canadians, including the federal government. There can be no question of the commitment of Canadians to conserving energy. The challenge is to find how all Canadians can be assisted in realizing that commitment.
A variety of steps are being taken to help Canadians achieve
our conservation goals. The few minutes available to me this
Adjournment Debate
evening are obviously insufficient to do anything more than note a few of these, but if the hon. member would like more details I shall be pleased to provide them to him.
The hon. member has inquired about legislation to promote conservation. As was set out in the Speech from the Throne, legislation will be brought forward soon to set mandatory efficiency fuel standards for automobiles, and our highly successful Canadian Home Insulation Program, CHIP, will be further improved.
With regard to co-operation with the provinces in conservation measures, in recent weeks the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) signed two federal-provincial agreements on energy conservation with the province of Manitoba. Existing agreements with Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia have been extended until details are worked out of new agreements which meet the specific needs of those provinces. We have federal-provincial conservation and renewable agreements with all other provinces and territories, and expect that the total expenditure on them will reach well over $200 million in the next four years, of which $114 million will be from the federal treasury.
Co-operation in the private sector has been equally encouraging. Members may be aware that voluntary task forces of business, working with the government, have already made major progress and show every promise of achieving even greater energy savings in the months and years ahead.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should perhaps add that the government itself has a vigorous energy conservation program which has achieved accumulated savings in the past four years of more than $100 million. This is a remarkable achievement, helping to indicate to all Canadians what can be done in this vital area of energy conservation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this adjournment debate tonight because of increasing dissatisfaction with answers we tend to get from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). I hope his parliamentary secretary will be more forthcoming. We had an example of what 1 mean about eight o'clock this evening which showed the difficulty of getting the minister to respond to questions.
My initial question, and the source of much concern to me tonight, was asked in this House some two weeks ago. At that time I brought to the attention of the minister the fact that there is a morale problem in his department in western Canada. The minister has over 5,000 employees in the four western provinces.
I was informed about mid-April for the first time, and on subsequent occasions by two or three of the minister's officials in his department, that there was a morale problem that was, in part, a consequence of what was reported to be the minister's decision to hire a defeated Liberal candidate from the

June 5, 1980
Adjournment Debate
riding of Calgary West to be a special adviser in the minister's office. Part of the discontent with that decision, which perhaps is not normal that civil servants should be so affected by such an appointment, was caused by the special adviser himself who, on April 7 in an interview conducted by a representative of the Calgary Herald, indicated that he was going to work in the minister's office in Winnipeg effective May 1 at a salary which was "the same as the salary he was receiving in his previous job". In that previous job this special adviser was the president of a small junior college in Calgary. The salary that was paid to him in that position was $50,000 a year.
I rose in the House to point out to the minister that there were morale problems in his department because the top civil servant in each of the four western provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, is classified as an SX-2. The salary range for these experienced people with heavy responsibilities for budget and other staff, begins just a little over $38,000. In this case the minister had appointed somebody without that background, without that experience and without those kinds of responsibilities to provide advice at a salary of some $50,000.
That situation is causing serious morale problems in the west. Those morale problems show themselves at the riding level in decreased service to people. If people do not work for an organization or for a minister in whom they can believe, or who treats his whole department fairly, then their morale goes down and their willingness to serve the Canadian public is adversely affected.
I think it might be in the minister's best interests, or the parliamentary secretary's best interests this evening, that if the minister was correct when he said in the House the other day that the $50,000 salary was not correct, it would be useful to morale in western Canada, if the parliamentary secretary could tell us exactly what that salary is.
All that the minister told us was that the salary was not $50,000. It could be $50,000 and one cent. It could be more than $50,000, it could be less. But I think it would be in the interests of this nation and a service to the people in western Canada if the minister or the parliamentary secretary could be forthcoming and tell us.
A little more than a week later I rose in this House as a consequence of the minister's statement to this House on Monday, and as a consequence of the press reports which followed. We heard a great deal of impressive rhetoric about the minister's concern for jobs for women. In news reports on Tuesday, the day after the minister's announcement, the minister was quoted in the press as saying that the program he announced in this House on Monday would create 81,000 jobs total. In that same press report his officials are reported as saying that the announcements made in the House on the same afternoon would create 31,000 jobs total.
The minister handed us background papers on that same day. If one was to total up all the subparts, they indicate that 192,000 jobs were created. I would hope that the parliamentary secretary could take this occasion this evening to tell us whether there were 31,000 jobs created, 81,000 jobs created,
or 192,000 jobs created. However, the really important part of that question is the fact that in the minister's background paper he estimates that of the jobs created, and it does not matter whether we are talking about the 31,000, 81,000 or 192,000, 12,200 of those will be filled by women. That is a number that almost boggles my mind, if I may use that expression. Whether it is 31,000, 81,000 or 192,000, 12,200 jobs is considerably less than half.
The minister has repeatedly stated that he cares about women and the employment opportunities available to them. Possibly the parliamentary secretary can tell us whether the minister will consider that whole job-creation package with a view to putting in some rules, regulations and procedures that will guarantee that at least half of the created jobs go to women. I wonder if the parliamentary secretary can give us an answer to that.

Mr. Speaker, if we add to the existing employment and training programs those announced on June 2, we note that more than 183,000 women will receive training or find employment this year.

June 5, 1980

work traditionally reserved for men, where salaries are generally higher. HEALTH AND WELFARE-MEDICARE PROGRAM-ANNOUNCED INCREASES IN PREMIUMS BY BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the minister for taking the trouble tonight to show up personally to answer the question I raised the other day about medicare in British Columbia.
Some say that most modern medical practices are some combination of band-aiding and pill-pushing, and criticize them on the ground that we tend to treat symptoms rather than causes. That may be true, that may be our emphasis, but that is not really the point. The point is that we are constantly hearing people complain about the soaring costs of health care. They seldom consider, though, the cost of being sick, and fail to recognize that a healthy society is money saved. 1 do not think the minister falls into that category, but there was a long and bitter fight to establish medicare in this country, and when we see evidence that it is being eroded, some of us are extremely alarmed. I know this feeling is shared by the minister.
I raise this matter because the spiralling health costs of the last few years have prompted certain provinces, which now have the right through certain legislation which was brought about in 1977, to deflect money normally going to medicare to other provincial priorities. Consequently, more and more of the costs of medical care and health care generally are being loaded upon the consumer of health care, often the old and the
Adjournment Debate
sick, and they are often one and the same. As a matter of fact the troika of being old, sick, and poor is not at all uncommon in this country. Sure, there should be more money going into preventive medicine, into more training in terms of improved lifestyles and into advice about fitness and all the rest of it. Nevertheless, whatever the failings of medicare may be in this country, most of us are extremely grateful that we have it, and we are extremely concerned if there are indications that we might lose it.
Some people say medicare costs too much. The most recent figures I have indicate that it costs about 7 per cent of our gross national product. That is a pretty fair chunk of money in this country, but in the United States there is only private medical care, and it is a tragedy to be sick in the United States. A lifetime of savings go down the drain if you are sick in the United States. The cost of medical care there is 9 per cent of the U.S. gross national product, so ours is better, cheaper, and the envy of North America.
In my question the other day I asked if the minister would get in touch with the government of British Columbia and tell that government that its regressive, reactionary increases announced recently by the British Columbia minister of health are unacceptable to the minister because they offend the guidelines of accessibility and comprehensiveness outlined in the principles of national health care.
1 would like to quote some of the figures which I read and which are associated with the costs announced. According to the Vancouver Sun of May 30, "Monthly medical premiums will be increased approximately 15 per cent". That does not perhaps seem alarming, except when you recall that it is 15 per cent on top of an already large increase. From 1974 to 1978 British Columbia premiums went up 50 per cent per family of four. British Columbia is not alone. In Ontario between 1974 and 1978 premiums went up 80 per cent. In Quebec they went up 88 per cent. In Alberta they went up 33 per cent.
As my party predicted during the debate on the established programs financing bill, money would be diverted, but we thought it would be the poorer provinces which would do the diverting. However, it has not been that way at all. It has been the more affluent provinces. So, naturally, we are alarmed.
To get back to the increases contemplated:
-$8.50 from $7.50 for a single person, to $17.50 from $15 for a couple and to $21.25 from $18.75 for a family.
Then there are increases for ambulances and daily charges for daily visits as well.
What I attempted to do in my question was to provide the minister with some impetus, some encouragement to let the province of British Columbia know how the federal minister, who is responsible for three-quarters of a billion dollars in health care, more accurately $750 million or so each year, or $778.8 million which was the figure I received from the minister's own department feels about increased user charges. During the campaign, and at the medicare conference on November 5, 1979, the minister said:

June 5, 1980
Adjournment Debate
I see now that two years ago when block funding for health care was instituted, the well-intentioned gamble has backfired.
At the same conference she went on to say:
Notice should be given of the commutation of block funding and the renegotiation of cost-sharing arrangements with the provinces. The federal government must re-establish control of the medicare program. That is the official policy of the Liberal Party of Canada.
She went on to say in Winnipeg, during the campaign, on January 21, 1980:
The federal government has the right to stop medicare financing if residents are not getting reasonable care when they need it.
She also said:
Opting out is a threat to universal accessibility when doctors "balance" or "extra bill" their patients.
These are all things that have come about in provinces which are putting the lid on health care. We have had all kinds of labour strife with health care workers, doctors and nurses in the richest parts of this country, and that is why 1 want the minister to remember it was a Liberal bill, this Established Programs Financing Act. It was designed by the Liberal government to put a cap on federal spiralling medicare costs. She should not wait for the Hall report, but let the provinces know that the way they are proceeding is completely unacceptable to the basic principles of medicare.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-MEDICARE PROGRAM-ANNOUNCED INCREASES IN PREMIUMS BY BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with regret that 1 have noted the action of the British Columbia government in increasing user charges under its hospital insurance plan and in increasing the premiums charged for coverage under its medical care insurance plan. What is most disturbing is that such increases and charges are not in the spirit or faith of medicare, which is free, good quality services to people wherever they live in Canada, in whatever province, and regardless of their income.
At the outset let me say that while 1 personally dislike very much these types of charges and the increases which are to commence on July 1, 1980, and 1 especially dislike the premium system which unfortunately is used in British Columbia and two other provinces in Canada, because premiums represent a regressive form of taxation, 1 must inform hon. members that, based on the information received, there is no action that the federal government can take immediately, such as withholding payment, and 1 will explain why.
Withholding payments can be done. It is the only tool provided in the legislation, a tool for the control of the use of the funds, but it can only be done based on the evidence that one or more of the five conditions is violated-the five principles on which medicare is based. 1 suppose it is fair to say that these principles or conditions are extremely general concepts and we are now faced with the problem in many provinces, unfortunately, where actions in the last two years, often in the last year and a half-unfortunately that is the case in British Columbia right now-may be breaching this concept, but withholding payment would cause a disruption of service to the people.
The previous government did appoint Mr. Justice Hall to make an inquiry which he will be completing, with recommendations, in a few weeks' time. There will just be the problem of translation left to finalize the inquiry and the publication of the report, and then I think it will be very urgent for all of us to make a great effort to save medicare, which I am sure we will do.
